routes.description: Establish a cumulative evidential route from the intelligibility of nature and mathematics, historically grounded miracle claims, moral experience, and the Christian treatment of evil toward rationally warranted Christian theism.
routes.successCriteria: Show that these considerations jointly fit Christian theism better than agnostic naturalism, while defending evidence-based faith, the coherence of divine action, and grounds for trusting divine goodness despite suffering.

motionBridge.description: Connect the cumulative force of scientific, mathematical, historical, moral, and existential considerations to an evidence-based commitment to Christian theism.

centralBridges.description: Explain why the intelligibility of nature and the effectiveness of mathematics are expected if a rational divine mind grounds both the cosmos and human reason.
Establish that Christian faith can be a reasoned commitment grounded in cumulative historical, experiential, and inferential evidence rather than unsupported assent.
Defend the epistemic coherence and historical importance of real divine miracles as signs disclosing the identity and purposes of Christ.
Account for moral evil through significant freedom and connect the cross, resurrection, judgment, and restoration to trust and hope amid suffering.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish successful methodological naturalism within science from the broader metaphysical claim that naturalism exhausts rational explanation.
Show how the theological meaning of Gospel narratives can depend upon, and be strengthened by, the reality of the events they report.

routes.description: Establish a cautious nonbelieving route by separating methodological science from theological explanation, distinguishing faith from empirical inference, interpreting miracle narratives without requiring supernatural events, and treating innocent suffering as evidence against confidence in a good God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the offered considerations do not warrant the specifically Christian conclusion because naturalistic inquiry does not require God, religious meaning can remain faith-based or nonliteral, and severe evil resists the proposed account of divine goodness.

motionBridge.description: Demonstrate that scientific order, religious experience, miracle narratives, and proposed answers to evil underdetermine the move from philosophical possibility to evidence-based Christian faith.

centralBridges.description: Explain why science may have Christian historical roots yet operate successfully through methodological naturalism without using God as an explanatory component.
Maintain a distinction between empirically supported scientific inference and the faith commitments through which Christian experience and doctrine are interpreted.
Offer an account of Gospel miracle narratives centered on moral, communal, and religious meaning without requiring supernatural violations or physically demonstrated events.
Show why the scale of innocent suffering and the costs imposed on victims challenge both the free-will defense and an evidential inference to divine goodness.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test natural-theology inferences by raising questions about the explanatory status of a designer and the evidential significance of defective features in creation.
Allow ultimate metaphysical questions and theological proposals while requiring that they remain distinct from scientific conclusions and open to criticism.

sections.title: Science, Mathematics, and the Intelligibility of Nature
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the historical origins, rational order, and mathematical tractability of science support a divine mind or remain compatible with methodologically naturalistic inquiry.

sections.title: Faith, Evidence, and Natural-Theology Inference
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether Christian commitment can arise from cumulative publicly assessable reasons or instead depends on a prior framework of faith that organizes experience and interpretation.

sections.title: Miracle Claims, Historical Reality, and Gospel Meaning
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether resurrection and Gospel signs function as coherent historical evidence of Christ or carry their religious significance without literal supernatural occurrence.

sections.title: Evil, Human Freedom, and Divine Goodness
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether atrocities and innocent suffering defeat confidence in a good God or can be situated within freedom, divine participation, final justice, and restoration.

sections.title: Science, Metaphysics, and Explanatory Limits
sections.rationale: This issue clarifies whether science's methodological boundaries leave rational space for theological explanation while avoiding an unwarranted transition from scientific practice to either theism or metaphysical naturalism.
